div.head: ECf 11.1 A 10
div.ab: Tres enim rex habere seruos debet, scilicet luxuriam, auaritiam et cupiditatem; quos si habuerit seruos, bene et illustre regnabit. Regno omnia debet premeditari; et hoc regis est. Quia ‘male cuncta ministrat impetus’; iuxta Euangelium ‘omne regnum in seipsum diuisum’. Hec hactenus.
div.note: Liebermann’s text transcribed from Gesetze I p. 636 (November 2026): read from the page images and checked against the scan’s own text layer, differences settled against the page.

This passage is not part of ECf or ECf retr: it is one of the additions of the London collection (Leges Anglorum s. XIII in. Londoniis collectae), which Liebermann prints in smaller type across the page, under ECf retr. 11, 1, and numbers 11, 1 A ff. The dictionary cites it as “ECf 11, 1 A …”, so it is kept with ECf here.
Liebermann marks “Euangelium” with a dagger for his marginal reference to Luke 11, 17.

note.seg: gegen des Königs iniquitas et insanitas lässt Lond den Papst eifern 11, 1 B 5 f.
Lond has the pope inveigh against the king’s iniquitas et insanitas, 11, 1 B 5 f.

div.ab: For the king ought to have three slaves, namely lust, avarice and greed; if he has them as slaves, he will reign well and gloriously. For the kingdom he ought to consider all things beforehand; and this is the king's part. Because ‘impulse manages all things badly’; according to the Gospel, ‘every kingdom divided against itself’. So much for this.

note.seg: Möglicherweise richtet sich die Zeile gegen König Johann im besonderen. — habere d. s., lux. — illustre in suo regnabit regno. Omnia [offenbar richtige Lesung; bessere so] — s.9 div. desolabitur Rs

Possibly the line is directed against King John in particular. — habere d. s., lux. — illustre in suo regnabit regno. Omnia [evidently the right reading; correct accordingly] — s.9 div. desolabitur Rs
